units.title: The brief
units.objective: Understand what the session is really about and the three claims you need to own.

blocks.v: The session title Scale Without Sacrifice: Architecting High Volume, Always-On Payment Systems is lifted almost word-for-word from a joint Icon Solutions / MongoDB whitepaper. That paper is a benchmark: Icon's IPF running on MongoDB Atlas, pushed from 500 to 6,000 payments per second, then deliberately broken to see what happens.
If you learn one artefact in this course, make it that one. The audience will treat it as the evidence base for everything claimed on stage.
Your credibility problem, narrowed
This is not "become a payments expert". It is three specific things:

v: Domain fluency — nothing said on the panel is new to you.
Architectural depth — you can defend the benchmark against a sceptical head of payments engineering.
A point of view that is yours — the data layer as the thing that decides whether a payment platform scales, stays up, and can feed an AI.

blocks.v: Three claims to own, in your own words

v: Scale is an architecture choice, not a hardware purchase. The benchmark scaled near-linearly by adding shards and pods, not by buying a bigger box — the opposite of how most incumbent payment engines were built.

Resilience is a data-model property. Zero data loss under an ungraceful node kill came from event sourcing plus a durable journal. Recovery meant rehydrating state from persisted events, not restoring from a backup.

ISO 20022 made payments a data problem. Rich, nested, versioned, jurisdiction-variant messages are what AI and agentic use cases feed on — and are exactly what relational payment schemas handle worst.

blocks.v: Work the modules in order. Modules 1–4 buy vocabulary and arguments; modules 5–7 buy defensible depth. The architecture only lands once you know what a payment actually has to do.

units.title: The payment lifecycle
units.objective: Narrate a payment end to end from memory, including the steps everyone forgets.

blocks.v: The four-step spine

v: Initiation — the instruction arrives from a channel: API, host-to-host file, branch, card terminal, scheme gateway.
Validation and enrichment — format, scheme rulebook, business rules, account and routing resolution, currency, calendar and cut-off logic.
Clearing — the exchange of payment instructions and the calculation of obligations between participants.
Settlement — the actual discharge of those obligations, in central bank money or commercial bank money.

blocks.v: The steps everyone forgets

v: Sanctions screening — a hard latency cost on every single payment, and a frequent source of holds.
Fraud scoring and Verification of Payee.
Limit and liquidity checks — can this customer, and can this bank, actually afford it right now?
Accounting and posting — usually the slowest and most legacy-bound integration in the platform.
Advice, reporting and reconciliation.
Exception handling — investigations, recalls, returns and repairs. Where most operational cost lives.

blocks.v: A payment is a state machine

Every payment must reach a terminal state — settled, rejected, returned. Non-terminal states (pending investigation, on hold, awaiting cover) are where risk accumulates. Hold on to this framing: everything in the architecture modules depends on seeing a payment this way.

units.title: The payments landscape
units.objective: Map the whole industry in one pass — instruments, schemes, business models, actors, money and rules — so that no term later in this course arrives unexplained.

blocks.v: Every other unit in this course goes deep on one part of payments. This one goes wide. It exists because the scheme names — instant payments, faster payments, request to pay, direct debit — turn up in the resources and the conversation long before anything explains how they relate to each other, and a map you can hold in your head is worth more at this stage than depth in any single corner.

blocks.v: The distinction that generates most of the rest is push versus pull. Push instruments put the payer in control at the moment of payment, so protection is thin afterwards. Pull instruments let the payee initiate without the payer present, so the scheme compensates with refund rights and dispute machinery. That single asymmetry explains why direct debit has an eight-week no-questions refund, why cards have chargebacks, and why instant credit transfers have neither — and therefore why authorised push payment fraud became a policy problem.

blocks.title: The uncomfortable truth to carry into every business case
blocks.v: Instant rails compress fees and destroy float. There is almost never an incremental-revenue case for instant payments infrastructure. The defensible cases are regulatory deadlines, cost-to-serve, and the ability to launch a scheme without running a programme. Saying this out loud, against your own interest, is one of the strongest credibility moves available to you.

What all of this demands technically
Everything above lands on the same platform, and it lands as two kinds of requirement. These are the headlines; modules 06 to 08 take each one apart.

v: Multi-scheme reachability and routing — which rail can reach this beneficiary, at what cost, within which cut-off.
A canonical internal model with per-scheme mapping in and out, so a new scheme is configuration rather than a rewrite.
The risk gauntlet in the payment path — sanctions screening, fraud scoring, Verification of Payee, limits, duplicate detection, each inside its share of the scheme's latency budget.
Real-time position keeping — can the customer afford it, and can the bank fund it on this rail right now, at three in the morning on a Sunday.
Mandate management for every pull instrument, and consent management for every agentic or open-banking one.
Exception handling — returns, recalls, investigations and repairs. The long tail with no SLA, the highest cost per item, and the worst tooling in most institutions.
Reconciliation against both the scheme and the ledger, because agreement with the counterparty is the only real proof of correctness.
Regulatory reporting and retention — every state transition reconstructable years later.
24/7/365 with no maintenance window. Instant schemes removed the batch night, and the IPR made availability a legal obligation rather than an SLA.
A decomposed latency budget. The scheme gives you a total; you divide it across screening, fraud, orchestration, persistence and posting.
Peak-to-mean design. Payments are spiky — salary dates, tax deadlines, Black Friday. Averages are a trap.
RPO zero. For money movement, correctness beats availability at the point where they conflict.
Elastic horizontal scale in units you can add without a migration.
Data residency — increasingly decisive in Europe, and cheaper to design in than to retrofit.
Observability and auditability — every state transition traceable, retained and reconstructable for a regulator or a dispute.
Demonstrable resilience. Under DORA, recovery behaviour is evidence you produce, not a property you assert.

blocks.title: The through-line
blocks.v: Every business model in this unit ends up as a non-functional requirement. A wallet that monetises float needs different data than an acquirer that monetises spread. An instant scheme's ten-second rule is a latency budget. An eight-week refund right is a retention policy. Regulation is a data requirement wearing a compliance hat. If you can walk that chain in both directions — from a commercial model down to an NFR, and back up — you can hold your own with anyone in this industry.

Where each thread continues: settlement and scheme mechanics in module 02, the rails market by market in 03, business models and institutions in 04, the regulatory clock in 05, payment hub architecture in 06, distributed architecture and integrity in 07, and the non-functional requirements and data argument in 08.

units.title: Rails — and the words everyone confuses
units.objective: Define a payment rail, and separate real-time, instant and account-to-account for good.

blocks.v: What a rail actually is

"Rail" is a metaphor that has hardened into a term of art. A payment rail is the combination of four things: a scheme rulebook (who may participate, what they must do, in what time, and who is liable), a message standard, the infrastructure that carries the messages, and a settlement arrangement that discharges the resulting obligations.

Miss any one of those and you do not have a rail. This is why people argue about whether stablecoins are a rail: the infrastructure and messaging exist, the rulebook and the settlement finality are the contested parts.

Rails are shared infrastructure. Products ride on them — Bizum, Zelle, Wero and a bank's own mobile app are not rails, they are propositions sitting on top of one. Keeping that distinction straight in conversation is a small thing that signals you know the domain.
Three words that are not synonyms

v: Real-time payments — generic: clearing and confirmation within seconds, around the clock. Beware that RTP is also a proper noun, The Clearing House's US network. When someone says "RTP" in a US context, ask which one they mean; the ambiguity causes real confusion in vendor conversations.

Instant payments — the European scheme and regulatory term, with a precise definition: funds available to the beneficiary within ten seconds, 24/7/365, and irrevocable once accepted. SCT Inst and the Instant Payments Regulation use it this way.
Account-to-account (A2A) — describes the route: money moves bank account to bank account without a card network in the middle. It says nothing about speed.

blocks.title: The distinction to hold on to
blocks.v: A2A is about topology. Real-time and instant are about speed and finality. They are independent axes. A standard SEPA Credit Transfer is A2A and slow. A card payment is fast to authorise and not A2A at all. SCT Inst happens to be both — which is exactly why people collapse the terms.

units.title: Topologies, processing modes and the acronym decoder
units.objective: Separate the three axes that get conflated — what sits between the endpoints, how instructions are processed, and when money becomes final — and decode the scheme acronyms without guessing.

blocks.v: The previous unit gave you one axis and one word for it: account-to-account. That word answers a question about topology — what sits between the payer and the payee. It is a real axis, but it is one of three, and most of the confusion in payments vocabulary comes from sliding between them mid-sentence. Batch, for instance, is not missing from the A2A grid because it was forgotten. It belongs to a different axis entirely.

blocks.title: Three independent axes
blocks.v: Topology — what sits between the endpoints, and who owns the relationship. Processing mode — whether instructions travel in files or one at a time. Settlement timing — when the money becomes final and who carries risk until then. They are genuinely independent: you can have any combination, and real instruments use most of them. Every time someone asks whether a payment is "real-time", ask which axis they mean.

blocks.v: Where A2A came from

Account-to-account is the oldest thing in banking wearing new clothes. European giro systems — postal giro from the early twentieth century, then bank giro — were account-to-account credit transfers by design: the payer instructs their bank to credit the payee's account, with no card, no scheme, and no intermediary owning the relationship. The SEPA Credit Transfer is that tradition standardised across a currency union.

What is new is the commercial framing. The term "account-to-account" comes from the merchant-acceptance world rather than from banking: it was coined to name an alternative to card acceptance. And it only became a real alternative when two things arrived together — open-banking APIs that let a licensed third party initiate a payment straight from the payer's bank account, and instant rails that made the money arrive fast enough for a checkout to complete. Neither the topology nor the rail was new. The combination, plus a licence to use it, was.

So when a vendor says "we do A2A", ask which of three things they mean: a PISP-initiated open-banking payment, a direct bank API integration, or a plain scheme credit transfer the merchant reconciles themselves. All three are account-to-account. Their economics, their failure modes and their reach are completely different.
Where topology is going

v: Variable Recurring Payments and commercial VRP — account-to-account with standing authority. This is the piece that has been missing: it closes the gap with direct debit and card-on-file, which is the only reason subscriptions still live on cards.
Interlinking — Project Nexus and bilateral scheme links, giving cross-border reach without anyone building a global scheme.

Tokenised deposits on a shared ledger — Swift's went into live pilot with 17 banks across six continents in July 2026. Banks keep the customer relationship while settlement moves to a shared ledger, which is a genuinely hybrid topology.
Retail central bank digital currency — the digital euro, if it ships, gives the public a direct claim on the central bank.

Agentic and delegated authority — AP2-style mandates introduce a party that is neither payer nor payee but acts for one of them. None of the topologies in the table above has a slot for that, which is exactly why the protocols are being invented rather than extended.

blocks.title: The CBDC point worth holding on to
blocks.v: Every topology in the table above ultimately routes a claim on a commercial bank. A retail CBDC routes a claim on the central bank itself. That is a change of topology, not a change of speed — and it is why the digital euro debate is about disintermediation and holding limits rather than about latency. If you only ever hear CBDC discussed as "faster payments", you are hearing it discussed wrongly.
Axis 2 — Processing mode: batch or single-message

Batch is not a speed, and it is not a generation of technology. It is a processing mode: whether instructions are accumulated into a file and handled as a group, or each one is carried end to end on its own with a response. That is independent of topology and independent of when money becomes final — which is why "batch versus real-time" and "real-time versus instant" are not the same comparison, and why batch never appeared in the account-to-account grid.

blocks.title: Batch is not legacy
blocks.v: It is the right answer whenever volume matters and latency does not — payroll, pensions, direct debits, supplier runs. Nobody wants payroll for fifty thousand employees carried as fifty thousand individual real-time messages, and no treasurer wants the intraday liquidity that would demand. The industry trend is more windows, not abolition. Treating batch as something to be eliminated is one of the fastest ways to sound naive in a payments conversation.
Axis 3 — Settlement timing

Covered properly in the next unit and in module 02, so briefly: gross settlement discharges each obligation individually and finally, usually in central bank money; net settlement accumulates obligations and offsets them in cycles, which is far cheaper in liquidity but leaves participants exposed to each other between cycles. This axis decides how much cash you must park and who is at risk while you wait.

blocks.title: The two rows that teach the most
blocks.v: Card payment is real-time at authorisation, batch at clearing and netted at settlement — so "is a card payment real-time?" has three different answers depending on which axis you mean. The promise is instant; the money is not, and that gap is precisely where chargebacks, settlement risk and working-capital cost live. UK Faster Payments is the mirror image: single-message processing but deferred net settlement. Instant to the customer, netted underneath. Instant at the service layer does not imply gross at the settlement layer.
The acronym decoder

v.def: Single Euro Payments Area — the regulatory and scheme space that makes a euro payment between member countries work like a domestic one.
SEPA Credit Transfer. The standard euro push payment: batch, next business day, no amount limit.
SEPA Instant Credit Transfer. The instant variant — ten seconds, 24/7/365, €100,000 scheme cap, mandatory for euro-area PSPs under the IPR.
SEPA Direct Debit. Core for consumers, with an eight-week unconditional refund right; B2B for businesses, with no refund right and mandate verification instead.
One-Leg Out Instant Credit Transfer — the EPC scheme for instant payments where one leg sits outside the EEA or in a non-euro currency. Governed by its own rulebook, separate from SCT Inst.
Original Credit Transaction — a push of funds to a card, used by Visa Direct and Mastercard Send for payouts, disbursements and remittances. Unrelated to OCT Inst.
Account Funding Transaction — the pull side of card push payments, funding a wallet or account from a card. AFT and OCT are typically paired to move money card-to-card.
SEPA Request-to-Pay. A messaging scheme, not a payment scheme — no money moves on it.
European Payments Council. Owns and publishes the SEPA scheme rulebooks.
Clearing and Settlement Mechanism — exchanges instructions between participants and calculates what each one owes. RT1, STEP2 and FedACH are CSMs.
Real-Time Gross Settlement — each payment settles individually and finally, usually in central bank money. T2 and Fedwire are RTGS systems.
Deferred Net Settlement — obligations accumulate and offset, settling in cycles. Cheaper in liquidity, but participants carry exposure to each other in between.
The Eurosystem's RTGS; the Eurosystem's instant settlement service; EBA CLEARING's instant CSM; EBA CLEARING's bulk CSM. RT1 settles through TIPS.
The UK trio: Faster Payments for instant retail, CHAPS for high-value RTGS, Bacs for three-day batch including Direct Debit.
Automated Clearing House — the US batch system, operated by the Federal Reserve as FedACH and by The Clearing House as EPN, under Nacha rules.
The Clearing House's instant rail, and Request for Payment — the request-to-pay message that runs on it.
Australia's New Payments Platform, India's Unified Payments Interface, Brazil's Pix, Switzerland's SIC. The domestic instant systems you will hear cited as benchmarks.
The EU Payment Services Directives and the incoming Payment Services Regulation — licensing, open banking, SCA and fraud liability.
Instant Payments Regulation — the EU law making instant euro payments mandatory, banning a price premium and requiring Verification of Payee.
Verification of Payee — the EU beneficiary name check under the IPR. Returns match, close match or no match, and shifts liability if the payer proceeds against a warning.
Confirmation of Payee — the UK equivalent, introduced earlier and under different rules. Same idea, different scheme: do not use the two names interchangeably.

Third-Party Provider, and its two flavours: Account Information Service Provider reads data on consent; Payment Initiation Service Provider initiates payments from the payer's account. PISP is the licence that makes A2A commerce possible.

Variable Recurring Payments — UK open-banking standing authority letting a payer approve repeated variable-amount payments within limits they set. The closest thing yet to a direct debit the payer actually controls.
Interchange Fee Regulation; Multilateral Interchange Fee; Merchant Service Charge — the EU cap, the fee it caps, and the all-in price the merchant actually pays.
Strong Customer Authentication; 3-D Secure, the protocol that usually delivers it online; and the card industry's data security standard — contractually mandatory rather than law.
Unique End-to-end Transaction Reference — the UUID that makes a cross-border payment trackable across every intermediary.
Swift's global payments innovation — tracking, transparency and confirmation across the correspondent chain. It gives you visibility, not speed.
Cross-Border Payments and Reporting Plus — the Swift ISO 20022 usage guidelines and the migration deadlines that run through 2028.
SEPA's collective term for rejects, returns, refunds, reversals and revocations. Where most operational cost lives.
Straight-through processing — a payment completing with no human touch. The straight-through rate is the industry's most quoted operational KPI.
Transfer of Funds Regulation — the EU rules requiring originator and beneficiary information to travel with a payment, including for crypto-asset transfers.
Open finance beyond payment accounts; auditable ICT resilience; and the EU crypto-asset regime covering stablecoin issuance, reserves and redemption.

blocks.title: Two acronym traps worth knowing before you hit them
blocks.v: OCT means two unrelated things. In a SEPA conversation it is One-Leg Out Instant Credit Transfer, an EPC scheme. In a card conversation it is Original Credit Transaction, a push to a card via Visa Direct or Mastercard Send. Context disambiguates, but only if you know both exist. CoP and VoP are not the same scheme. Confirmation of Payee is the UK's beneficiary name check; Verification of Payee is the EU's under the IPR. Same idea, different rulebooks, different match semantics and different liability. Using one name for the other in front of a European payments audience is a small tell.

This decoder covers scheme and regulatory acronyms. Module 10 carries a separate glossary of operational terms of art — cut-off, nostro, prefunding, straight-through rate, scheme pack — which is the vocabulary you use in conversation rather than the names you have to look up.

units.title: Clearing is not settlement
units.objective: Distinguish RTGS from deferred net settlement, and explain how instant schemes sit between them.

blocks.v: Two settlement models

v: RTGS — real-time gross settlement. Every payment settles individually and finally in central bank money. No netting, no credit risk between participants, but high liquidity demand. T2 in the euro area, Fedwire in the US.
DNS — deferred net settlement. Obligations accumulate and net down, settling in cycles. Liquidity-efficient, but participants carry exposure to each other between cycles. ACH and CHIPS work this way.

blocks.v: Where instant payments sit

Instant schemes are a hybrid: instant and final to the customer, but underneath either prefunded (participants park cash at the clearing and settlement mechanism) or net-settled on a short cycle. This is why prefunding is a real treasury cost and a common objection in any instant-payments business case.
Push versus pull

Credit transfer, direct debit, card authorisation-then-capture, request-to-pay. Each has a different failure mode and a different dispute regime — which is exactly where card economics and account-to-account economics diverge. A card chargeback and a SEPA direct debit refund look similar to a customer and nothing alike to a bank.

The single most useful sentence you can carry out of this unit: a customer can be told a payment is confirmed before settlement has occurred, and someone is carrying risk in that gap. Know who, for each rail.

units.title: Inbound and outbound flows
units.objective: Describe both directions of a payment platform, and explain why they are not mirror images.

blocks.v: Payment platforms are almost always discussed as if there were one flow. There are two, they have different failure modes, and the difference is the single most useful thing to understand before looking at any architecture.
Outbound — you set the pace

v: Instruction arrives from a channel — API, file, branch, mobile.
Validate, enrich, resolve routing: which rail can reach this beneficiary, and what does that rail cost and require?
Risk gauntlet — sanctions, fraud, Verification of Payee, limits, duplicate detection.
Liquidity and limit check: can the customer afford it, and can the bank fund it on this rail right now?
Debit the customer, or reserve the funds.
Format to the scheme and submit.
Wait for the status message, then confirm to the customer — or unwind everything you just did.

blocks.v: The hard part is step seven. Between submission and confirmation there is a window where the outcome is genuinely unknown, and your system must model that as a state rather than an error.
Inbound — someone else started the clock

v: The scheme delivers a pacs.008. You did not choose when.
Validate, screen, resolve the beneficiary account, check its status — closed, blocked, dormant, wrong currency.
Decide: accept, reject, or accept-without-posting — within the scheme SLA.
Post the credit and make funds available.
Send the pacs.002 status back.

blocks.title: The asymmetry is the whole point
blocks.v: Outbound, you control the pace and can queue work. Inbound, a clock someone else started is already running, and under the Instant Payments Regulation you cannot decline to be reachable. That is why availability requirements bite hardest on the inbound path, and why inbound screening has to be pre-computed or extremely fast — you cannot ask the sender to wait while you think.
The flows people forget

v: On-us payments — both legs at the same institution. They never touch a scheme, so they are routinely missing from capacity models and reconciliation designs, and then someone notices that a third of volume was never counted.
Returns and R-transactions — an outbound payment that comes back is an inbound event on a payment you thought was finished.
Recalls — a camt.056 arriving about a payment you sent is an inbound request that triggers outbound work, and needs a human decision inside a scheme deadline.
Investigations — the long-tail flow with no SLA, the highest cost per item, and the worst tooling in most banks.

blocks.title: The confusion this unit exists to kill
blocks.v: Instant payments is a service. RTGS is a settlement mechanism. They are not alternatives and they are not the same kind of thing — they answer different questions and sit at different layers. An instant payment is what the customer buys; RTGS is how the resulting obligation is discharged. TIPS is a settlement service that applies the RTGS model to instant payments. Once you separate these layers, most of the vocabulary stops fighting you.

units.title: Net settlement versus instant schemes
units.objective: Explain why instant finality changes the liquidity model, and what that does to the architecture.

blocks.v: Deferred net settlement, and why it was invented

In a netting system, obligations accumulate over a cycle and are then offset multilaterally: if you owe me 100 and I owe you 90, only 10 moves. The liquidity saving is enormous — netting routinely reduces the funds that must actually settle by an order of magnitude — which is precisely why ACH, CHIPS and STEP2 are built this way.

The price is risk between cycles. Participants are exposed to each other until settlement completes, which is why netting systems carry net debit caps, collateral requirements and loss-sharing arrangements describing what happens if a participant fails before the cycle settles. Those arrangements are the least glamorous and most important part of the rulebook.
Instant schemes cannot net

If every payment is final the moment it is accepted, there is no cycle to net across. Each one must be backed by real funds at the moment it happens — 24 hours a day, including weekends when the RTGS system that would normally top you up is closed.

blocks.title: The architectural consequence
blocks.v: In a batch world the liquidity question is answered once per cycle by a treasury team. In an instant world it is answered per payment, in milliseconds, at three in the morning on a Sunday. Real-time position keeping stops being a treasury report and becomes a hot path in the payment engine — which is to say, it becomes a data problem.

Weekend and holiday liquidity is the practical pain nobody mentions in vendor decks: the instant rail is open, the RTGS that funds it is not, and someone has to have parked enough cash on Friday to survive until Monday without over-funding and carrying the cost.

blocks.v: Direct debit is a pull

The creditor initiates, on the authority of a mandate the debtor granted earlier. Everything distinctive about direct debit follows from that inversion: the payer is not present at the moment of payment, so the scheme protects them afterwards instead.

v: SDD Core — consumers. An unconditional refund right for eight weeks, no reason required, and thirteen months for an unauthorised collection. That refund right is the product.
SDD B2B — businesses. No refund right, and in exchange the debtor's bank must verify the mandate before paying.
The mandate machinery — Unique Mandate Reference, Creditor Identifier, amendment and cancellation handling, and a pre-notification obligation before each collection.

R-transactions — rejects, refusals, returns, refunds and reversals, each with a different originator, a different deadline and a different liability outcome. This is where the operational cost of direct debit lives.

blocks.v: Request to Pay is a message, not money

SEPA Request-to-Pay (SRTP) is a messaging scheme layered above the payment rails. The payee asks the payer to pay; the payer accepts, rejects, defers or pays in part; and if they accept, a perfectly ordinary credit transfer — usually an instant one — does the actual moving. No money travels on the RtP scheme itself.

blocks.title: Why this matters strategically
blocks.v: Direct debit gives control to the creditor. Request to Pay hands control back to the payer while keeping the creditor's ability to prompt. Pair RtP with an instant credit transfer and you get billing with the creditor's certainty of being asked, the payer's control, immediate finality and no refund liability — which is why it is a structural threat to both direct debit and card-on-file billing.
Why it is architecturally awkward

An RtP is a conversation, not a transaction. It has its own lifecycle — issued, accepted, rejected, deferred, partially accepted, expired — that is separate from the lifecycle of the payment it eventually triggers, and the two must be correlated afterwards. It is a state machine sitting on top of another state machine, with a many-to-one relationship between them. Rigid schemas handle this badly, which is a point worth having ready.

The UK equivalents to know by name: Pay.UK's Request to Pay, and variable recurring payments, the open-banking mechanism that lets a payer authorise repeated variable-amount payments within limits they set — the closest thing yet to a direct debit the payer actually controls.

units.objective: Know the timing rules of both schemes precisely enough to reason about a latency budget.

blocks.v: SCT Inst

v: Ten seconds maximum, measured from the moment the originator's PSP accepts the transaction as valid to the beneficiary PSP confirming that funds are available.
Twenty seconds is the hard ceiling for exceptional cases — not a second budget you may plan against.
24/7/365, with every participant technically obliged to be available.
€100,000 scheme maximum per transaction, reviewed annually, with participants free to agree higher limits bilaterally or multilaterally.

The originator's PSP cannot unilaterally reject once the timer is running — it must wait for a negative confirmation or the timeout. This is the rule that forces you to model "outcome unknown" properly.

blocks.v: FedNow

v: A 20-second timeout clock, configurable by the Reserve Banks.
The clock starts from the message creation timestamp, not from when FedNow receives it — so your own clock skew and internal queuing eat the budget before the network sees the message.

The receiving institution may reserve 1–5 seconds for its own response processing. If insufficient time remains for that reserved window, FedNow rejects the message immediately rather than forwarding it.
The receiver answers accept, reject, or accept without posting (ACWP) — the escape hatch for when it will honour the payment but cannot complete posting inside the window.
On timeout, FedNow rejects with a pacs.002. A resubmission needs a new message identifier, or it is rejected as a duplicate.
If no confirmation arrives, wait until 25 seconds have elapsed before sending a pacs.028 status request — sending it earlier risks creating the duplicate you are trying to avoid.

blocks.title: The reading that matters
blocks.v: Both schemes make the unknown outcome a first-class case, and both defend against duplicates explicitly — new message IDs on resubmission, a mandatory wait before a status enquiry. That is a rulebook telling you to build idempotency and a status-request pattern. Take it literally; it is the same requirement the integrity unit arrives at from the engineering side.

The other practical point: ten seconds is the budget for the whole chain, not for your hop. Screening, fraud scoring, account resolution, posting, and the network itself all come out of it. Your internal share is a fraction — which is why sub-30-millisecond persistence in the benchmark is worth talking about, and why anyone quoting a database latency without stating the scheme budget it fits inside is not really making an argument.

units.title: Europe
units.objective: Name the scheme, the infrastructure and the settlement model for any euro payment.

blocks.v: Schemes

v: SCT — SEPA Credit Transfer. The standard euro credit transfer.
SCT Inst — the instant variant. Ten seconds end to end, 24/7/365.
SDD Core and SDD B2B — SEPA Direct Debit for consumers and businesses, with different refund rights.
One-Leg Out (OCT/OLO) — scheme variants for payments where one leg sits outside the EEA.

blocks.v: Infrastructure

v: T2 — the Eurosystem's RTGS, where high-value euro payments settle in central bank money.
TIPS — TARGET Instant Payment Settlement. Instant settlement in central bank money, 24/7/365, operated by the Eurosystem.
RT1 and STEP2 — EBA CLEARING's instant and bulk clearing and settlement mechanisms.

blocks.v: The domestic overlays

Wero, from the European Payments Initiative, is the sovereignty play — an attempt to build a European account-to-account alternative to the card schemes. It has to displace entrenched national incumbents to succeed: iDEAL in the Netherlands, Bizum in Spain, Blik in Poland, Swish in Sweden. Treat its prospects as an open question rather than a foregone conclusion in either direction.

units.title: The United States
units.objective: Explain the US rail landscape and, more importantly, why instant adoption has been slow.

blocks.v: Five rails

v: ACH — Nacha-governed, batch, with same-day options. Enormous volume, very low cost.
Fedwire Funds — the Fed's RTGS for high-value payments, now ISO 20022-native.
CHIPS — privately operated, netted, high-value.
RTP — The Clearing House's instant rail, launched 2017.
FedNow — the Federal Reserve's instant rail, launched July 2023.

blocks.v: The adoption gap is the story
RTP does roughly 47× FedNow's volume at about 1/26th the average ticket. That is two different use-case portfolios, not a winner and a loser.

The bigger number: the US runs at 0.12 fast payments per person per month, against 35 in Thailand, 27 in Brazil and 13 in Sweden. The honest reason is that Zelle, same-day ACH, card push payments and wallets already deliver an instant feel. There is no burning consumer need for true real-time settlement.
Cards still dominate the revenue pool

Interchange, scheme fees and acquiring. The US has no interchange cap; Europe has had one since 2015. That single regulatory difference explains most of the divergence in merchant behaviour and account-to-account adoption between the two markets — and it is the bridge into the business-models module.

units.title: Gateways, and where every acronym sits
units.objective: Place gateway, RTGS, ACH, RT1, STEP2 and TIPS on one map and never confuse them again.

blocks.v: What a payment gateway is

The term comes from card acceptance: the component that takes a payment request from a merchant's checkout, secures and tokenises the card data, and routes it to an acquirer or processor. Crucially, a gateway does not clear or settle anything. It is an access layer — connectivity, protocol translation, security and routing.

The word has since spread. Banks talk about a SWIFT gateway, a scheme gateway, a FedNow gateway. The meaning is consistent: a boundary component that fronts a network so the systems behind it do not each have to speak that network's protocol. When someone says gateway, the question to ask is which boundary.
Do not confuse it with payment orchestration, which sits a layer above and routes across multiple gateways and PSPs — choosing between them on cost, authorisation rates or availability.

blocks.v: Now the acronyms, placed

v: RTGS — both a settlement model (gross, immediate, final, in central bank money) and the systems that implement it: T2 in the euro area, Fedwire in the US. Settlement layer.
ACH — automated clearing house. Generically a batch, netted clearing system; in the US specifically the networks operating under Nacha rules, FedACH and EPN. Clearing layer.
STEP2 — EBA CLEARING's pan-European bulk CSM for SEPA credit transfers and direct debits. Europe's closest equivalent to an ACH: netted, cyclical. Clearing layer.
RT1 — EBA CLEARING's instant CSM for SCT Inst and One-Leg-Out instant transfers. Real-time gross, not netted. Clearing layer, settling in central bank funds.
TIPS — the Eurosystem's instant settlement service. It spans both layers: it clears and it settles, in central bank money, on Dedicated Cash Accounts.

blocks.title: The relationship people get wrong
blocks.v: RT1 and TIPS are often described as competitors, and for instant clearing they are. But RT1's technical account migrated into TIPS in December 2021, so RT1 settles through TIPS and a participant can manage liquidity for both in one place and exchange instant payments across them. "Competing but interconnected" is the accurate phrase, and using it correctly is a quiet credibility signal.

One more distinction worth keeping sharp: TIPS is not simply "the European FedNow". FedNow is an operator-run clearing and settlement service that institutions join directly. TIPS is a settlement service that both institutions and other clearing mechanisms connect to. The topologies differ, and so do the liquidity models.

units.title: Cross-border
units.objective: Explain correspondent banking, the G20 targets, and what is actually changing.

blocks.v: How it works today

Correspondent banking: a chain of banks holding accounts with each other. Nostro is our account with them; vostro is their account with us. A cover payment moves the funds along the chain while the instruction travels over Swift. The costs are the chain length, the trapped liquidity in nostro accounts, and the compliance check at every hop.
De-risking has shortened the chains and concentrated corridors, which is good for cost and bad for access — one of the reasons the G20 got involved.
The G20 roadmap
Four targets, and you should know all four: cost, speed, access, transparency. Swift gpi and the UETR addressed transparency and much of speed. Cost and access remain stubborn.
What is changing

v: Interlinking — connecting domestic instant systems directly rather than routing through correspondents. Project Nexus is the multilateral attempt; bilateral scheme links already exist.

Tokenised deposits — Swift's shared blockchain ledger went into live pilot on 9 July 2026 with 17 banks across six continents, moving funds continuously before final settlement through existing systems. Concept to activation in nine months.
Stablecoins — now a regulated instrument in both major markets, and therefore a genuine cross-border option rather than a crypto curiosity. Covered in the regulation module.

units.title: The five revenue lines
units.objective: Explain whose P&L a platform decision hits.

blocks.v: Technology arguments lose to economics arguments inside a bank. If you can name the P&L line, you stop being the database person and start being the industry principal.

v: Transaction fees — per-payment pricing, heavily commoditised in Europe.
Interchange and scheme fees — the card stack. Capped in the EU since 2015, uncapped in the US.
Float and net interest income — earnings on balances held between instruction and settlement.

blocks.title: The uncomfortable truth about instant payments
blocks.v: Instant rails destroy float and compress transaction fees. There is almost never an incremental-revenue case for instant payments infrastructure. The defensible cases are regulatory deadlines, cost-to-serve, and the ability to launch a new scheme without running a programme. Saying this out loud, against your own interest, is one of the strongest credibility moves available to you.
Cost-to-serve is the real metric

v: Cost per transaction at peak, not at average.
Cost of a failed payment — typically an order of magnitude higher than a successful one.
Cost of an investigation, and the straight-through rate that determines how many you get.
Cost of absorbing a scheme mandate release, twice a year, forever.

units.title: Who is who, and what their licence lets them do
units.objective: Name the institution types in any payment flow and say what each is licensed and exposed to.

blocks.v: Two rules make this whole taxonomy tractable. The licence determines what you are allowed to do. The risk you bear determines what you buy. Everything below is an application of those two.
The account-holding side

v: Banks / credit institutions — take deposits, hold customer accounts, and can hold accounts at the central bank. Direct access to RTGS settlement is the deepest structural privilege in payments, and it is what everyone else is ultimately renting.

Payment institutions (PIs) — licensed under PSD2, and under PSD3 in a regime merged with e-money. They execute payments but cannot take deposits. EU policy has been steadily opening payment-system access to them, and under the Instant Payments Regulation non-bank PSPs pick up instant obligations from April 2027.
E-money institutions (EMIs) — issue electronic money against received funds. PSD3 folds them into the payment-institution regime, which is one of the package's quieter but more consequential changes.
Banking-as-a-service providers — rent their licence and rails to non-licensed brands. The regulatory question is always who is actually accountable when something fails.

blocks.v: The card side

v: Issuer — gives the cardholder the card, carries credit and fraud loss.
Acquirer — contracts with the merchant, carries merchant credit risk and chargeback exposure.
Scheme — Visa, Mastercard and the domestic schemes. Sets rules, sets interchange, moves no money itself.
Processor — does the technical work on behalf of issuers or acquirers. A large share of the industry's actual transaction processing sits here, invisibly.
Payment facilitator (PayFac) — aggregates sub-merchants under its own acquiring relationship, taking on their onboarding and fraud risk in exchange for speed and margin.
Merchant of record — the legal seller. Owns tax, compliance and chargeback liability for the sale. Distinct from who processes the payment, and routinely confused with it.

blocks.v: The open-banking side

v: AISP — account information service provider. Reads account data with the customer's consent.
PISP — payment initiation service provider. Initiates a payment directly from the customer's bank account, bypassing the card rails entirely. This is the licence that makes A2A commerce possible.
TPP — the umbrella term for both. FIDA extends the same logic beyond payment accounts into the wider product estate.

units.title: The Instant Payments Regulation and Verification of Payee
units.objective: Explain the most operationally interesting requirement in the whole European package.

blocks.v: The obligations
Why VoP is the interesting one

Verification of Payee checks the beneficiary name against the IBAN before the payment is sent, and returns one of three outcomes: match, close match (with the actual name disclosed), or no match. The payer then chooses whether to proceed — and if they proceed against a warning, liability shifts.
Three things this forces on a bank, and they are all data-platform capabilities:

v: A real-time queryable beneficiary directory, available 24/7 with sub-second response. A nightly batch file cannot satisfy this.
Fuzzy name matching at scale, tuned to avoid both false negatives (which annoy customers) and false positives (which defeat the purpose).
A durable audit record of what was shown to the payer and what they chose, retained for the life of any potential dispute.

blocks.title: The sanctions wrinkle
blocks.v: The IPR also changed sanctions screening for instant payments: rather than screening every transaction in-flight, PSPs verify their own customer base against sanctions lists at least daily. This is a meaningful architectural change — it moves a latency cost out of the payment path and into a periodic data process.

units.title: PSD3, PSR, FIDA and DORA
units.objective: Hold a credible view on the European regulatory package without over-predicting the politics.

blocks.v: PSD3 and the PSR

Political agreement was reached in late November 2025; publication in the Official Journal is expected during 2026. The PSR is a regulation and applies directly, roughly 18 months after entry into force. PSD3 is a directive and needs national transposition, putting realistic applicability at around Q2/Q3 2028.
The substance:

v: Extended fraud liability, reaching in certain cases to online platforms that fail to act on known fraud after notification.
Collaborative fraud-data sharing between PSPs via a dedicated mechanism — a data-sharing obligation with real architectural implications.
SCA rework — clearer rules, more flexible exemptions, stronger verification for high-risk transactions.
IBAN/name verification extended to all credit transfers, not just instant ones.
Licensing harmonisation — e-money institutions folded into the same regime as payment institutions.
Transparency — upfront disclosure of FX margins, which directly attacks one of the five revenue lines in the business-models module.

blocks.v: FIDA

The open finance regulation sitting alongside PSD3, extending data access rights beyond payment accounts into the wider financial product estate. Where PSD2 gave third parties access to accounts, FIDA extends the principle — with compensation arrangements, which PSD2 lacked.
DORA — the one that matters for your session

Already applying. DORA turns resilience from an engineering preference into an auditable obligation: ICT risk management, incident classification and reporting, third-party oversight including critical ICT providers, and threat-led penetration testing.

blocks.title: Why this is your bridge

Who may issue — and what that means for a bank considering a tokenised deposit instead.

units.title: The canonical hub anatomy
units.objective: Whiteboard a payment platform from memory and defend every box on it.

v: Channel and adapter layer — host-to-host, API, file, scheme gateways. Normalises everything into a canonical internal model, which in practice means ISO 20022 plus extensions.
Validation and enrichment — format, scheme rulebook, business rules, account and routing resolution, currency and calendar/cut-off logic.

Risk gauntlet — sanctions screening, fraud scoring, Verification of Payee, limits, duplicate detection. Each with its own latency budget, and each capable of parking a payment in a non-terminal state.

Orchestration engine — the workflow driving the payment through those steps, per scheme and per product, with compensation paths. In IPF this is configurable flows built in IPF Studio; in Temenos and Oracle it is the payment order engine and process framework.
Liquidity and settlement — position keeping, prefunding, RTGS interaction, netting, cut-off management, cover.
Accounting and posting — usually the slowest, most contended, most legacy-bound integration in the platform.

units.title: The architectural patterns
units.objective: Discuss the benchmark's design decisions, not just its results.

v: Event sourcing. Persist the sequence of events and derive state from them. This is why the benchmark could kill a node and rehydrate in-flight payments with zero loss. Know the trade-offs too: replay cost, schema evolution, and the need for snapshots.

CQRS. Separate the write path (an event journal tuned for durable append) from the read path (an operational data store tuned for query and reporting). In the benchmark these were two separate MongoDB clusters — five shards and six shards — for exactly this reason.

Idempotency and effectively-once processing. Networks retry; money must not. Idempotency keys, deduplication windows and the outbox pattern combine to give effectively-once semantics over at-least-once delivery.

Back-pressure. A payment hub is only as fast as its slowest downstream. Back-pressured streams — IPF's connector framework does this — stop a slow core banking system from becoming a cascading failure.
Sagas and compensation. There is no distributed transaction spanning a scheme, a core and a sanctions engine. There is a saga with reversals, and the reversals are the hard part.
State machines and terminal states. Every payment must reach one. "No payment left in limbo after a node failure" is the claim you are on stage to defend.

blocks.title: The mechanism, stated properly
blocks.v: Zero data loss on an ungraceful kill did not come from a backup. Shard rebalancing redistributed in-flight transactions, and each surviving node rebuilt payment state by replaying persisted events. State was rehydrated, not restored. That distinction is the whole argument, and it is the sentence to have ready.

units.title: The canonical model, ISO 20022, and XML versus JSON
units.objective: Explain why ISO 20022 is not a canonical model, and what a good one carries.

blocks.v: Why a canonical model exists at all

A payment platform speaks many formats in and many formats out. Map each input directly to each output and you have N×M mappings to build and maintain. Introduce one internal representation that everything maps into and out of, and you have N+M. That internal representation is the canonical model, and the arithmetic is the entire justification.
The tempting mistake
"We will just use ISO 20022 as our canonical model." It is rich, it is standard, and it is already on the wire. It is also the wrong choice, for four reasons worth being able to give quickly:

v: It is a message standard, not a state model. A pacs.008 describes an instruction at a moment in time. Your platform needs lifecycle, decisions, risk scores, internal enrichment, operator actions and audit — and the message has nowhere to put any of it.

There is no single ISO 20022. Every scheme publishes its own usage guideline — CBPR+, SCT Inst, FedNow, TCH — with different mandatory fields, different code lists and different length constraints. They conflict. Picking one as canonical means the others become second-class.
It versions annually. You will support several releases at once, indefinitely.
Not everything is ISO. ISO 8583 for cards, remaining MT traffic, proprietary bank APIs, and flat files will all outlive your project.

blocks.v: What a good canonical document carries

v: Normalised common fields — the parts every payment has, whatever arrived: parties, amounts, currency, references, dates.

The original payload, verbatim. Keep what actually arrived. It is the forensic record when a dispute, a regulator or an investigation asks what was really sent — and once you have discarded it, no amount of reprocessing brings it back.
Mapping provenance — which rule, which version, which agent or which human produced each derived field. This is what makes an automated transformation auditable rather than merely convenient.
Lifecycle state and decisions — where the payment is, what was decided, by whom, and why.

blocks.title: The two problems this actually solves
blocks.v: Rich to constrained: a payment carrying structured ISO 20022 remittance data crosses onto a legacy rail that cannot hold it, and the data is silently truncated. Sparse to rich: a bandwidth-optimised ISO 8583 message from a point of sale lacks the granularity downstream ISO 20022 compliance requires. A canonical document that keeps both the original and the normalised view lets you detect the first and enrich for the second — neither of which is possible once you have flattened everything into the target format.
XML versus JSON — and the claim to stop repeating

ISO 20022 is a model, held in a central repository. XML is its classic serialisation; JSON is an officially supported alternative syntax. So "ISO 20022 means XML" is simply wrong, and correcting it gently is a nice way to demonstrate you have read the standard rather than a summary of it.

head: XML
JSON
rows: XSD schema validation, namespaces, mature and strict
JSON Schema — later to the party, now broadly sufficient
High — tag-heavy, large on the wire
Lower, and closer to how services already work
Deep in banking middleware and scheme tooling
Native to APIs, and maps directly onto a document store
On the wire, because the schemes require it
Internally, because that is what your services and storage want

blocks.v: The practical stance most modern platforms land on: XML at the boundary, document-shaped JSON inside. The mapping between them is a real cost, and it is precisely why you build the canonical model once rather than once per scheme. It is also the cleanest version of the data-platform argument — a nested, optional-heavy structure that varies by scheme and versions every year is what a document model is for. The relational alternative is a wide sparse table or a join-heavy schema, and either way each annual release becomes a migration.

The failure mode to name if someone pushes back: over-normalising. A canonical model that discards what it could not classify is worse than no canonical model, because it destroys evidence while looking tidy.

modules.title: Distributed architecture and data integrity
modules.subtitle: How horizontal scale actually works, and how you keep money correct while doing it

units.title: Horizontal scale and sharding
units.objective: Explain scale-out properly, and defend a shard key choice to someone who has designed one.

blocks.v: Scale up versus scale out

Vertical scaling buys a bigger machine. It works until it doesn't: there is a largest available box, the price curve turns vicious well before that, and the whole thing remains a single failure domain. Horizontal scaling adds more machines and spreads the data across them. The ceiling moves from "the biggest server you can buy" to "how many servers you are willing to run".

This is the difference the benchmark was built to demonstrate. Going from 500 to 6,000 payments per second was not a hardware upgrade — it was adding shards and pods, with latency staying flat until peak.
How sharding works

v: Data is partitioned across shards by a shard key. Each shard is itself a replica set, so distribution and redundancy stay separate concerns — you are not trading one for the other.
Data is divided into chunks by key range, and a balancer moves chunks between shards to keep the distribution even.

A query that includes the shard key is targeted to a single shard. A query that does not is scatter-gather across every shard. In a payment platform, lookups by UETR or end-to-end identifier must be targeted, or your read path degrades as you grow — which is the opposite of the point.

blocks.v: Choosing the shard key — the decision that decides everything

head: Property
What you want
What goes wrong
rows: Too few values caps how far you can ever split
One value takes most writes and its shard becomes the bottleneck
A monotonically increasing key sends every new write to one shard

blocks.title: The classic payments mistake
blocks.v: Payment identifiers are usually sequential, and creation timestamps always are. Shard on either and every single new payment lands on the same shard — you have bought a distributed system and kept a single write bottleneck. The fixes are a hashed shard key, or a compound key with a high-cardinality prefix. Being able to name this trap unprompted is worth more than any amount of general enthusiasm for scale-out.
Zone sharding and data residency

Zones pin key ranges to specific regions. Put a jurisdiction attribute in the shard key, map zones onto regions, and one logical cluster serves several jurisdictions without any customer's data leaving its own. This is the cleanest answer to European data-residency requirements, and it beats the usual alternative of running a separate stack per country.

State the cost honestly when you present it: a write that must cross a region boundary pays the latency. The design question is whether the payment's write path ever needs to cross one — and for most retail flows it does not.
Replica sets, and what durability means

v: A replica set is a primary plus secondaries. Writes go to the primary and replicate.

Majority write concern means an acknowledgement only comes back once a majority of members hold the write. That is what "zero RPO" means in practice — not a slogan, a setting with a measurable latency cost.
Failover is automatic — around five seconds in the benchmark, with payment processing continuing across it.
Read preference can route reporting and analytics to secondaries so they never contend with the payment write path.

blocks.v: The benchmark as a worked example

Two clusters, split by access pattern: a five-shard event journal, append-heavy, and a six-shard operational data store tuned for query — roughly 236,000 and 196,000 operations per second respectively, on M80-class shards of 32 vCPU and 128 GB. At peak the hot shard sat near 50% CPU and the storage engine's write queue stayed at zero.

That last detail is the one to quote. Aggregate throughput hides saturation; per-shard utilisation and an empty write queue are what actually demonstrate headroom. Anyone can publish a big number — showing the per-shard curve is what makes it evidence.

units.title: Integrity, consistency and idempotency
units.objective: Explain how a distributed payment system stays correct — and get idempotency exactly right.

blocks.v: Money is not like other data. A lost message in most systems is an inconvenience; here it is a payment that either happened twice or never happened, and someone has to find out which. Everything below is about making that question answerable.
Durability first

v: Majority write concern plus journaling — the write is acknowledged only once a majority of replica-set members have it durably. Survives the loss of the primary. This is the concrete meaning of RPO zero.
Majority read concern — you never read data that could still be rolled back, which matters enormously when the thing you are reading decides whether to send money.

blocks.v: Atomicity, and why the data model decides it

A single-document update is atomic. So if a payment's state lives in one document, almost every state transition needs no distributed transaction at all — the hardest problem in the system disappears by modelling. Multi-document ACID transactions are there for the cases that genuinely span documents, such as a ledger entry and a state change that must move together.

blocks.title: The design rule
blocks.v: Make the atomic unit match the business unit. A payment is one thing conceptually, so make it one thing physically. This is the strongest practical argument for a document model in payments, and it is about correctness, not convenience — which is why it lands with engineers when "flexible schema" does not.
Idempotency — four mechanisms, and one distinction
Networks retry. At-least-once delivery is all you ever get. Effectively-once processing is what you build on top of it.

v: Idempotency key. The caller supplies a key; you store it under a unique index. On a replay you return the original result instead of re-executing. The unique index does the enforcement — the database, not the application logic, which is the point.
Deduplication window on scheme identifiers. Message ID, end-to-end ID, UETR. The schemes assume you do this: FedNow rejects a resubmission that reuses a message identifier.

Monotonic sequence per aggregate in the event journal. Appending event N+1 fails if N+1 already exists, so a duplicated command physically cannot append twice. Event sourcing gives you this almost for free.

The outbox pattern. Write the state change and the outbound message in one atomic write, then publish separately. This is what prevents both "posted but never sent" and "sent but never posted" — the two most expensive bugs in payment engineering.

blocks.title: The distinction that separates people who have done this from people who have read about it
blocks.v: Idempotency is a property of the operation, not the request. Retrying "debit account X by 100 under key K" is safe. Retrying "add 100 to the balance" can never be made safe, whatever you wrap around it. Model commands with identity, not deltas.
Consistency across services

v: There is no distributed transaction spanning a scheme, a core banking system and a sanctions engine. There is a saga: a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions.

The compensations are the hard part, because a compensation can itself fail. Every reversal path needs the same durability and idempotency guarantees as the forward path, and it usually gets a fraction of the design attention.

Change streams let downstream processes react to a committed state change without polling and without dual writes — the trigger is the durable write itself, which removes a whole class of race condition.

blocks.v: Two things to say precisely

v: Exactly-once does not exist on the wire. Effectively-once is achievable at the endpoint. Saying it that way marks you out; saying "we guarantee exactly-once delivery" marks you out too, in the other direction.

Reconciliation is the backstop, not a fallback. Even with everything above, you reconcile against the scheme and the ledger, because the only real proof of correctness is agreement with the counterparty. Any design that treats reconciliation as an admission of failure has misunderstood the problem.

blocks.v: Notice that the rulebooks arrived at the same place from the other direction: new message identifiers on resubmission, a mandatory wait before a status enquiry, a status-request message defined in the standard. The schemes are specifying idempotency and asking you to implement it. That is a good line.

v: Availability: 24/7/365 with no maintenance window. Instant schemes removed the batch night there was to hide in. Active-active across availability zones, and increasingly across regions because of DORA.

Latency budget: the scheme gives you a total — often a handful of seconds end to end — and you decompose it across screening, fraud, orchestration, persistence and the core. The benchmark's sub-30 ms persistence at peak matters precisely because it leaves the budget to the risk checks.
Throughput profile: payments are spiky. Salary dates, tax deadlines, Black Friday, scheme go-lives. Design for peak-to-mean ratio, never for average.
RTO / RPO: for money movement, RPO must be zero. Say it that way — it reframes the entire database conversation from performance to correctness.
Elastic scale: horizontal, in units you can add without a migration. Near-linear scaling is the claim; per-shard CPU and insert rates rising proportionally is the evidence.
Data residency and sovereignty: increasingly decisive in Europe. Keeping data in-jurisdiction while running one logical platform is a differentiating capability, not a checkbox.
Observability and auditability: every state transition traceable, retained, and reconstructable years later for a regulator or a dispute.

units.title: The data-platform argument
units.objective: Make the case for a document data platform without sounding like a vendor.

blocks.v: ISO 20022 messages are deeply nested, optional-field-heavy, versioned annually and varied by scheme and jurisdiction. Modelling that relationally means either a wide sparse table or a join-heavy schema — and either way, every scheme release becomes a migration.

A document model stores the message as it is, evolves without downtime, and lets the event journal and the operational data store be tuned independently. Add horizontal sharding for throughput, replica sets with majority write concern for zero-RPO durability, zone sharding for residency, and search and vector indexes in the same platform for fraud and investigation — and you have removed most of the reasons a payment platform needs four separate data stores.

blocks.title: The ordering matters
blocks.v: Lead with durability, not flexibility. Flexibility sounds like a developer convenience; zero RPO under an ungraceful node kill sounds like a control. Make flexibility your second reason, never your first.
The operational data layer pattern

The ODL consolidates payment state that would otherwise be scattered across the hub, the core, the screening engine and the case management system. It is what makes real-time investigation, natural-language querying and AI feature extraction possible — and it is the reason the AI module works at all.

Single region. No core banking system in the loop. Synthetic load. Say all three before someone else does — then reframe: the value is not the headline number, it is the shape of the curve. units.title: Agentic AI on the cross-border exception path
units.objective: Make the most concrete agentic argument available in payments today — and know why it is the exception path.

blocks.title: Lead with this framing
blocks.v: Straight-through processing is already automated. Nobody needs an agent for the payments that work. The value sits in the few per cent that fail, and that is also where the unstructured data lives — investigation notes, correspondent emails, free-text remittance fields, local market practice. Which is why the exception path is a retrieval and reasoning problem rather than a rules problem, and why it is the first place agents genuinely earn their keep.
The problem, sized

v: Failed payments cost the global economy more than $100 billion a year. That is the number to have ready.
Legacy cores do not natively support ISO 20022, so data is lost and humans intervene.
Institutions run several standards at once — ISO 20022, ISO 8583, residual MT, local real-time APIs — each with its own schema and translation layer.
Even inside ISO 20022, regional market practice and optional elements create local dialects that cause rejection and rework.
Rich nested structures such as complex invoice references are destroyed when forced into rigid relational tables.

blocks.v: Four agent patterns worth naming

head: Pattern
What the agent does
What it needs underneath
rows: Flags fields at risk of truncation, enriches sparse messages from internal profiles, transforms semi-structured data into ISO 20022
The original payload preserved, plus similar past exceptions retrievable by meaning
Embeds unstructured case notes and finds conceptually related past cases rather than keyword matches

Compares true corridor cost — fees, FX spread, on-chain gas — against policy and recommends a settlement path
Live telemetry captured as time series, and policy the agent can read
Proposes field mappings between standards for a human to approve
Mapping provenance, so every proposal is auditable

blocks.v: What the data layer has to provide

v: A canonical document holding the native payload and the normalised fields together — the foundation from the architecture module, now doing work.
Vector search over investigation notes and past exceptions, so retrieval is by conceptual similarity rather than string matching.
Multi-document ACID transactions, because an agent-driven update to a ledger entry and a payment state must move together or not at all.
Change streams and stream processing to trigger workflows the moment state changes, without polling and without dual writes.
Global clusters and zone sharding for corridor latency and data residency.
CQRS to keep the agent's read traffic off the payment write path — the referenced payment data store sustains roughly 10,000 writes per second behind 1,000 payments per second.

blocks.v: Governance is the part that sells it

Every AI input and output logged and linked to an approval; mapping provenance recorded so any transformation can be traced to the rule, agent or human that produced it; schema validation and encryption enforcing policy. Human-in-the-loop is a design requirement here, not a disclaimer — and the audience you will be speaking to cares far more about that than about model capability.

The strategic frame is worth borrowing: this is a control-preserving alternative to rip-and-replace. A bank does not have to replace its core to get here; it has to stop throwing away the data its core cannot hold. That argument works in a room full of people who have been told to modernise and have no appetite for another five-year programme.

One honest caveat to carry: none of this removes the human from a payment that has already failed a regulatory check. Agents compress investigation time and improve first-time-right rates. Claiming more than that in this room will cost you.

units.title: The questions that will test you
units.objective: Rehearse delivery, not content. Answers that open with a concession land better in this room.

blocks.v: Practise these out loud. Every one opens by conceding something true — that is what makes the rest credible.

v.q: "6,000 TPS is a synthetic benchmark. What does that have to do with my bank?"
v.a: Concede first: controlled benchmark, single region, twelve processing steps, no core banking system in the loop. Then reframe — the value is not the headline number, it is the shape of the curve. Near-linear scaling from 500 to 6,000 with flat latency means capacity is a procurement decision, not a re-architecture. That is the property a bank should test for in its own environment, and the benchmark tells you what to measure.

v.q: "Why would I put payments on a document database?"
v.a: Because ISO 20022 is a nested, optional-heavy, annually versioned document format, and because the write path and read path in a payment hub want opposite things. Then the durability point, which is the one that matters: replica sets with majority write concern give you zero RPO, and the ungraceful-kill test is the evidence. Do not lead with flexibility — lead with durability, and let flexibility be the second reason.

v.q: "Our bottleneck is the core banking system, not the payment engine."
v.a: Agree immediately and completely. This is true at almost every bank, and saying so buys more credibility than any statistic. Then the architectural answer: back-pressured streams so the hub degrades gracefully rather than cascading, an operational data store that absorbs read load the core would otherwise carry, and event sourcing so posting can be asynchronous without losing the audit trail. The hub's job is to stop being the constraint and to stop the core from becoming a single point of failure.

Answer with the thing you would tell a bank not to do. For example: replacing a payment engine to chase instant-payments revenue is usually a bad business case in Europe, and the defensible cases are cost-to-serve, regulatory deadlines and the ability to launch a scheme without a programme. Specific, slightly against interest, and instantly disarming.

v.q: "How do you handle data residency across a multi-region deployment?"
v.a: Zone sharding: the shard key includes a jurisdiction attribute, zones pin ranges to regions, and one logical cluster serves multiple jurisdictions without data leaving them. Then the honest caveat — cross-region writes cost latency, so the design question is whether the payment's write path ever needs to cross a boundary, and usually it does not. Naming the cost is what makes the answer credible.

v.q: "What does agentic AI actually change for a payment service provider?"
v.a: Two things, concretely. First, authorisation stops being a single moment and becomes a mandate with constraints that must be stored, checked and revoked — infrastructure most PSPs do not have. Second, transaction volumes decouple from human attention, which breaks the assumptions behind both fraud models and capacity planning. Then be honest that the standards are unsettled and most of the industry is at pilot stage.

v.q: "Everyone claims linear scaling. Why should I believe this one?"
v.a: Because the evidence is per-shard, not aggregate. CPU and insert rates rose proportionally per shard across the ladder, the WiredTiger write queue stayed at zero, and there was roughly 40–50% headroom at the top of the range. Aggregate throughput numbers hide saturation; per-shard utilisation does not. Then invite the test: run the same ladder on their own topology.

units.title: Your ninety seconds
units.objective: Draft and rehearse the one uninterrupted stretch you will get.

blocks.v: Whatever the panel format, you get one uninterrupted stretch. This is the shape it should take. Write it in your own words and say it aloud until it stops sounding written.

v.v: The sacrifice. For twenty years, payment platforms traded one thing for another — throughput for resilience, resilience for agility, agility for control. Name the trade the audience actually lives with.

Why the trade is now unaffordable. Instant schemes removed the batch window. The IPR made 24/7 a legal obligation. DORA made recovery auditable. ISO 20022 multiplied the data. None of these are choices.
The evidence. Six thousand payments a second, half a second end to end, node killed under live load, ninety seconds to recover, zero payments lost. Scale-out, not scale-up.

The mechanism. Event sourcing and CQRS over a distributed, sharded data layer. State is rehydrated from persisted events, not restored from backup. That single design decision is what makes "zero loss" a property rather than a promise.

The consequence. The same data foundation that survives failure is the one that feeds fraud models, investigations, and next, agent mandates. You do not get an AI strategy in payments without solving the data layer first.
Hand back with a question for the panel rather than a summary. It signals confidence and keeps you in the conversation.

units.title: Terms of art
units.objective: Use the vocabulary naturally. Misusing a term costs more than not using it.

v.def: Unique End-to-end Transaction Reference — the UUID that makes a cross-border payment trackable across every intermediary.
The interbank customer credit transfer. The workhorse message; know its structure.
Request to cancel a payment. The opening move of most investigations.
SEPA's collective term for rejects, returns, refunds, reversals and revocations. Where most operational cost lives.
Real-time gross settlement versus deferred net settlement — individual finality versus netted cycles.
Clearing and Settlement Mechanism. TIPS and RT1 are competing CSMs for euro instant payments.
SEPA scheme variant for payments where one leg sits outside the EEA.
Verification of Payee — the IBAN/name check mandated by the IPR since October 2025.
The scheme or correspondent deadline after which a payment moves to the next value date. Instant rails removed it; everything else still runs on it.
Our account with them / their account with us. The plumbing of correspondent banking.
Cash parked at the CSM so instant payments can settle outside RTGS hours. A real treasury cost, and a common objection.
A pluggable module implementing one scheme's rulebook, messages and certification. IPF's unit of extensibility.
Operational data store or layer — the read-optimised projection of payment state. The read half of CQRS.
US corporate control where issued payment files are matched before release. Comes up in US fraud conversations.
Percentage of payments needing no human touch. The most quoted operational KPI in the industry.
In AP2, the verifiable credential recording what a user authorised an agent to do. The new unit of consent.
The funds movement that accompanies a payment instruction along the correspondent chain.
MongoDB's storage-engine write backlog. Zero under load is the evidence that persistence is not the bottleneck.
